title: Nepal’s Deadliest Glacier Collapse Exposes Larger Risks - Columbia University
description: Nepal’s Deadliest Glacier Collapse Exposes Larger Risks  Columbia University
publisher.title: Columbia University
full_article:
In late August, a glacier partially collapsed on Langtang Lirung, the highest peak in the Langtang Himal subrange of the Himalayas, located just 12 miles away from the Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and Tibet. Around 400 people were preparing to cross the border that morning. Within an estimated seven minutes after the initial collapse, flood water hit the border at over 100 miles per hour. The 65-foot border control gate was swept away with the surge and carried over 60 miles downstream along the Trishuli River.

The impact was catastrophic. The flood water would destroy an estimated 7,500 homes in Nepal as well as several bridges and roads, and severely damage a number of hydroelectric power stations. The death toll has risen to over 1,500 people, with some 5,600 still missing. Nepalese officials estimate the cost of rebuilding will amount to $4.71 billion.

Security camera footage of the flooding hitting the border crossing. Credit: Seewhyso / Wikimedia Commons

Scientists have slowly unpacked how a disaster of this magnitude could have unfolded with so little warning. Roughly 7 billion cubic feet of glacial ice and rock collapsed, falling thousands of feet into a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, a mass large enough that the U.S. Geological Survey initially mistook the event for a 5.2 magnitude earthquake. In the days after the flood, the cause of this event remained unclear, but scientists now believe that climate change may have played a large part: a World Weather Attribution analysis released in mid-September concluded that years of rising temperatures had thinned the glacier and thawed permafrost deep in the surrounding bedrock, making the slope far more prone to collapse than it might have been otherwise. Some scientists initially speculated the collapse could have been a product of warming temperatures weakening the ice. Others pointed to instability in the underlying bedrock. The research that has emerged since showed that both analyses were true: thawing permafrost had been loosening the fractured rock beneath the ice.

Given Nepal’s history, the volume of floods that ensued led glaciologists to first speculate that the event might have been a product of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF). Nepal is home to several thousand glacial lakes, making outburst floods a reasonably frequent occurrence. As a result, a great deal of Nepal’s glacial hazard work is organized around these lakes: their volumes and stability are monitored, giving time to act should the risk of a breach rise. In July 2025, an outburst flood came down this same corridor, killing nine people and damaging several of the same projects.

Ice-rock avalanches, however, are harder to forecast than GLOFs. Existing systems “cannot catch rapid micro-scale events like cloud bursts or glacial floods in advance,” said Milind Kudapa, a graduate research assistant at Columbia Climate School, in an interview with GlacierHub. India and Nepal have roughly five to 10 automated weather stations per 10,000 km², compared with around 120 in Switzerland, a country less than a third of the size of Nepal, where a similar collapse at Blatten in 2025 saw 300 people evacuated nine days in advance. Langtang had no such system, and the glacier collapse came with no advance warning. The floods that followed raced through the Lhende Khola Valley and into the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor, destroying the flood warning gauges before they could send an alert.

Satellite imagery of the aftermath in the Lhende Khola Valley. Credit: USGS EarthExplorer / Wikimedia Commons

The scale of the tragedy in the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor was in part due to a lack of forecasting, but also a product of the amount of infrastructure located within the valley. Fourteen hydropower facilities stood along the 60km corridor that the floods followed. One of the first projects hit was Upper Trishuli 1, a 215-megawatt run-of-the-river power plant that was scheduled to finish construction in December of this year. When the facility was struck, only about 16 minutes after the initial collapse, 1433 workers were inside—300 of whom were suspected to be trapped in access tunnels running deep underground, blocked from exiting by debris and thick mud. This mud also impeded the machinery needed for rescue efforts; over 800 workers were rescued, but the others are presumed dead.

Nepal has lost just over a tenth of its national grid capacity (around 431 megawatts). Its hydroelectric power industry, almost all of which is nestled within the Himalayas, is central to Nepal’s economic future. Steep glacier-fed river corridors like the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli offer the best hydropower conditions in the country: a sharp drop over a short distance, and meltwater that keeps the rivers running even through the dry season. Nepal generates almost all of its electricity this way, and both India and China have poured foreign direct investment into new projects along these rivers. These sites tend to be economically productive, but they are also some of the most at risk.

The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure estimates that around $124 billion of Nepal’s infrastructure is threatened by climate-driven disasters. Annually $760 million is spent on disasters around the country, costs that drastically outweigh the amount Nepal has allocated towards its national disaster fund. “Nepal’s challenge isn’t only a lack of financial tools,” said Nitin Magima, who works on the financial instruments sector team at Columbia Climate School’s National Center for Disaster Preparedness, “it’s about how these tools are arranged in advance.” By the end of September, insurers had paid out about Rs 6.75 million ($44.911 USD) against nearly Rs 21 billion ($139.7 million) in preliminary claims. Closing the gap, Magima argued, “means agreeing beforehand which layer pays for which loss, and how quickly.”

Syafrubesi, one of the villages the flood swept through, pictured in 2023. Credit: Pustam.EGR / Wikimedia Commons



There is an imbalance between the amount of money being funneled into renewable infrastructure projects in ecologically sensitive areas, and the lack of sufficient risk management techniques being used to forecast potential disasters within those areas. “We are building into the hazard zone faster than we are learning to see it,” said Kudapa, “and it only takes a small trigger to turn decades of construction into a few minutes of debris.”

Beyond forecasting, options for hydropower include conducting more extensive geological evaluations of the valleys plants are placed within, and altering the location and density of plants along rivers such that a single disaster is less likely to destroy a series of plants at once. This is a factor that was largely ignored along the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor: all the projects there were assessed individually, with no basin-wide assessment of cumulative risk. Ram Prasad Dhital, chairman of Nepal’s Electricity Regulatory Commission, has argued that construction standards for hydropower plants will have to rise nationally, a cost that will ultimately fall upon the consumer: electricity is expected to become at least 10–12% costlier, even as Nepal sells surplus power to India and Bangladesh.

After the July 2025 flood, the corridor was repaired within months, but were the deeper causes addressed? There’s a road in Manali that the river destroys every monsoon but it “is rebuilt every time at the exact same place,” says Kudapa. Likewise, the Rasuwagadhi plant, rebuilt at the same site after 2025, was destroyed again this August. This time the damage is an order of magnitude larger, and how long rebuilding will take—and the extent to which it will occur at all—remains to be seen.

title: Nepal Seeks Additional Air Routes from India Amidst Strategic Discussions - Ratopati
description: Nepal Seeks Additional Air Routes from India Amidst Strategic Discussions  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Among the issues that are always at the center of discussion and interest before almost every Prime Minister of Nepal's visit to India is the international air route between the two countries.

Although Nepal has been demanding additional air entry points from India for more than a decade, it has not reached a concrete conclusion. In the context of recent signals that India might grant an air route from Mahendranagar in return for a request for an entry point from Bagdogra, what are the real conditions, possibilities, and challenges of Nepal's aviation sector? Rato Pati has discussed this topic with former Director General of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CANA), Rajkumar Khatri.

In the context of the Prime Minister's visit to India, the issue of air routes (air routes) is always raised. This time too, there are signals that India will ask for an entry route from Bagdogra and Nepal will be given a route from Mahendranagar or Bhairahawa. As someone who has worked in leadership positions in the aviation sector for a long time, how do you view the historical background of the air route that Nepal has been demanding from India and the current possibilities?

– Nepal's demand for an air entry route through Mahendranagar in India is not new; this issue has been raised for about 10 to 12 years. In fact, we have been demanding four air entry routes from India: Mahendranagar, Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj, and Janakpur. However, India has always postponed it, citing its security sensitivities. Specifically, the Indian side argues that there would be 'security threats' due to the Air Force base in India's Gorakhpur region and other strategic structures.

When I myself was the Director General of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, I had direct dialogues and discussions with Indian officials on this matter. In the discussions at that time, they complained that there was no other problem in giving us the route, but only some complexities in terms of security and air traffic safety. However, I still remember that when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Nepal, he took this issue seriously and publicly committed that the air route would be implemented within the next six months. I was working in Civil Aviation at that time.

But unfortunately, about 12 years have passed since that commitment was made, and it has not materialized to this day. Now, again, in the context of the Prime Minister's visit, the signal that the Mahendranagar route will be opened, if it is truly implemented, will definitely bring multifaceted and far-reaching benefits to Nepal.

What is the current status of international air travel in Nepal? Which entry points are currently used by aircraft coming to Nepal from various parts of the world, and what is the compulsion of using India's airspace?

Looking at the current state of international air entry points into Nepal, our airspace appears to be quite limited and dependent on a single point. Especially for all international aircraft coming to Nepal from the west, south, and the Middle East, 'Simara' is currently the only available entry point through India's airspace. Any aircraft coming from Europe, Gulf countries, or other Western countries must pass through India's airspace to enter Nepal, and there is no other option besides Simara.

Not only that, but aircraft coming from China also have to enter near Kakadvitta in eastern Nepal and then proceed to Simara instead of landing directly at Kathmandu airport, and then circle back to land at Kathmandu airport. Besides this, all other international airlines coming via India's airspace must use Simara as their entry and exit point. Apart from managing our own internal airspace, India has not provided any other entry point besides Simara for international flights using Indian airspace, thus Nepal's entire international aviation system is confined to the narrow scope of a single entry point.

What are the technical, time, and economic losses incurred when aircraft coming from West Asia, Europe, or the West have to come via Simara? How does this affect airline companies?

With only one Simara entry point, airline companies are bearing an extremely heavy technical and economic burden. Let's understand this with a simple example.

Suppose an aircraft is coming to Nepal from the Middle East or Europe, passing near Nepal's western airspace. If the Mahendranagar route were open, that aircraft could enter directly from western Nepal and land in Bhairahawa or Pokhara within minutes. But in the current situation, even an aircraft coming from the west has to travel all the way east to Simara via India, parallel to Nepal's western airspace. Then, an aircraft that needs to go to Bhairahawa or Pokhara has to circle back west after entering Simara. This is a paradoxical situation.

Flying for 25 minutes longer than the scheduled time directly affects the aircraft's maintenance schedule and the crew's duty hours. It is precisely this unnecessary time and high operating cost that has led foreign airline companies to show reluctance in flying to the airports built in the western and central regions of Nepal, as circling via Simara would result in significant commercial losses for them.

Thus, having to unnecessarily go to Simara and return wastes about 20 to 25 minutes of extra time on each flight. In the field of aviation, a delay of 20 to 25 minutes is a significant loss. On one hand, passengers and aircraft time are wasted, and on the other hand, the aircraft's fuel consumption increases significantly.

In today's competitive aviation market, fuel cost is the biggest expense for airline companies. Moreover, the technical operating life of the aircraft and the crew's flight hours also have a certain limit. Flying for 25 minutes longer than the scheduled time directly affects the aircraft's maintenance schedule and the crew's duty hours. It is precisely this unnecessary time and high operating cost that has led foreign airline companies to show reluctance in flying to the airports built in the western and central regions of Nepal, as circling via Simara would result in significant commercial losses for them.

Nepal had demanded four air routes from India. But now only the Mahendranagar route is being discussed more. Even if only Mahendranagar is given immediately without giving the routes for Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj, and Janakpur, how much benefit will it bring to Nepal?

Certainly, in the past, we had demanded all four air entry points from India: Mahendranagar, Bhairahawa, Nepalgunj, and Janakpur, and in principle, obtaining all those routes would be even better for Nepal. However, looking at the current diplomatic dialogue and my understanding of the situation, it does not seem that the Indian side will be ready to grant all four routes immediately. Rather, India appears to be more positive and agreeable to granting the air entry route from Mahendranagar in the immediate term. Discussions and dialogues on the remaining three routes will continue gradually in the future.

But the reality is that if India grants us only the entry route from Mahendranagar immediately, it will be a matter of great benefit for Nepal and the Nepali aviation sector. This is because Mahendranagar is the most strategic and shortest entry gate for flights coming from the west, Europe, and the Middle East. Once Mahendranagar is opened, the compulsion of taking the long detour via Simara will end. This will specifically breathe life into the operation of international airports in the western region.

For aircraft coming from the eastern region, i.e., Thailand, Bangkok, or Malaysia, the route naturally falls near the eastern or southern Simara, so there is not much difference. However, for the Middle East and European markets, which are our main international air traffic and where migrant workers and tourists travel, opening the Mahendranagar route will prove to be a sufficient and revolutionary step.

If India opens the Mahendranagar air route, how can the Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa and the Pokhara International Airport, which are currently non-operational and idle, become operational?

The opening of the Mahendranagar route is like a lifeline for the Bhairahawa and Pokhara international airports. The Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports, built with billions of investments, are almost idle due to the lack of regular international flights. The main reason why foreign airline companies are not interested in flying to these two airports is the extra time, fuel cost, and commercial loss incurred by having to circle via Simara. When the route for direct entry from Mahendranagar opens, aircraft coming from the Middle East and Europe will be able to land directly in Bhairahawa and Pokhara without going to Simara.

This will save airline companies 25 minutes of time and a large amount of fuel, making flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara commercially profitable for them. Especially, the Bhairahawa airport has the potential to operate at an even faster pace and more effectively than Pokhara. The availability of the Mahendranagar route will generate interest among foreign airlines, and they will be ready to operate regular flights. Furthermore, the full operation of Bhairahawa and Pokhara will greatly help in reducing the excessive air traffic pressure at Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport. However, opening the route is not the only solution; we also need to be able to sell those airports commercially, i.e., market them effectively.

What other internal preparations and improvements need to be made by the Nepali government for the marketing and passenger attraction of the Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports after obtaining the Mahendranagar route?

Obtaining an air route is a technical aspect, but for the airport to operate sustainably, there must be a guarantee of passengers and business. Let's take the Bhairahawa airport as an example. The largest segment of passengers traveling from Nepal to the Middle East, i.e., the Gulf countries, consists of Nepali migrant workers going abroad for employment. Currently, migrant workers from western Nepal are compelled to come to Kathmandu to visit manpower companies, undergo health check-ups, obtain labor permits, and complete other administrative procedures. When the work is done in Kathmandu, they do not return to take a flight from Bhairahawa; they fly from Kathmandu.

Therefore, if the Government of Nepal provides all government and private services related to foreign employment, such as labor offices, manpower branches, medical centers, and visa facilitation mechanisms, in the Bhairahawa and Butwal areas, not a single migrant worker from the western region will have to come to Kathmandu. They will be able to fly easily from Bhairahawa.

Only after ensuring passenger traffic in this way will foreign airline companies schedule regular flights there. And, on the other hand, the government and tourism sector bodies must play an active role in promoting tourism in Pokhara and Bhairahawa, ensuring easy access to hotels and transportation, and strong marketing of those airports internationally. If these internal homeworks are completed, Nepal can fully leverage the benefits of the Mahendranagar route.

There is a discussion that India has asked for an entry point from Bagdogra in the east instead of or along with Mahendranagar. It is heard that the Nepali delegation has said that they will respond only after studying this matter in Nepal. What kind of impact could granting India an entry point from Bagdogra have on Nepal's security or air travel?

A final decision has not yet been made regarding Bagdogra, and it is a natural diplomatic process for the Nepali delegation to say they will decide after returning to Nepal and studying the technical aspects. However, based on my long experience in the aviation sector, I do not think that granting India an entry point from Bagdogra will pose a significant security threat or problem to Nepal. From a security perspective, there is no situation where such a serious challenge would arise from Indian flights over Nepal. The main question is whether Indian aircraft entering from Bagdogra will disturb Nepal's internal or international flights, which is a technical matter.

In my understanding, it does not seem that India will bring a large number of its aircraft into Nepal's airspace from Bagdogra. Possibly, India might have requested a small portion of Bagdogra only for facilitating flights in a specific and limited area of Bihar state. However, as I am no longer in an executive role and do not have the actual current air traffic data before me, the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and aviation experts will surely conduct a thorough technical study and evaluation. If the technical study by the experts shows that granting entry from Bagdogra will not significantly affect Nepal's air safety and internal flight management, and if we get the Mahendranagar air entry point in return, it will be a very beneficial agreement for Nepal. In diplomacy, one should not hesitate to 'give and take' for mutual benefit.

Besides air routes, there are many other issues in Nepal's aviation sector. There are complaints that India has not provided necessary support to the Pokhara and Bhairahawa airports and that there is inequality in air connectivity between Nepal and India. What could be other major aviation sector agendas that Nepal should raise during this visit?

Certainly, not just air routes, but Nepal should also raise the issue of 'air connectivity', i.e., bilateral flight access, with India with equal vigor in the dialogue. As far as the discussion about India not cooperating with the Pokhara airport is concerned, the root of that is mainly this air route itself. The problem in connectivity seems to have arisen precisely because India has not granted this route. If India opens the Mahendranagar route, many connectivity problems will automatically find a solution, and we can expand connectivity with other countries as well.

Therefore, if the Government of Nepal provides all government and private services related to foreign employment, such as labor offices, manpower branches, medical centers, and visa facilitation mechanisms, in the Bhairahawa and Butwal areas, not a single migrant worker from the western region will have to come to Kathmandu. They will be able to fly easily from Bhairahawa.

And, a more serious and direct issue is the lack of flight permits for Nepali airline companies to fly to major Indian cities, including Delhi. Currently, there is significant inequality in flight permits between Nepal and India. Nepal has welcomed all types of Indian government and private airlines with open arms. We have granted as many flight permits as possible to Indian airlines like Indigo, Air India, etc., to fly to Kathmandu and elsewhere without any restrictions. But in return, India has not allowed private Nepali airline companies to fly to Delhi.

This unequal treatment must be ended, and the Government of Nepal must raise this issue seriously at the diplomatic level.

What is the actual situation regarding Nepali airline companies not being able to access Indian airspace and airports?

Looking at the current reality, only the national flag carrier Nepal Airlines Corporation (RNAC) has received permission to fly from Nepal to India's capital, Delhi. Capable and large private airline companies in Nepal have not been able to get permission to fly to Delhi, even though they want to. For example, Buddha Air has been trying to fly to Delhi for a long time, but India has only granted permission for Varanasi, not Delhi. This permission has not been granted to date.

Similarly, Shree Airlines has also been trying for a long time with full preparation for flights to Delhi. It is heard that assurances have been given verbally by the Indian side that Shree Airlines will be granted permission, but official written documents have not yet been received.

Thus, Nepali private airline companies are forced to sit idle, unable to fly internationally despite investing heavily, because India has not granted them flight permits. Meanwhile, Indian airlines are unilaterally capturing the market in Nepal. Even if a large private company in Nepal brings a new aircraft and wants to operate flights to major Indian cities, there is uncertainty about whether India will grant slots and permits. According to the principle of reciprocity, just as Nepal has welcomed Indian airlines openly, India should also grant Nepali private airlines easy flight permits to major destinations like Delhi.

This issue must be raised as a priority during high-level government visits.

India is the main source of Nepal's tourism market. If Nepali airline companies get easy access to cities like Delhi and the Mahendranagar route opens, what impact will it have on Nepal's overall tourism and economy?

As you said, the main and sustainable source market for our tourism industry is neighboring India. India has a large middle-class population that wants to come to Nepal for travel and religious tourism. When air connectivity between Nepal and India strengthens, i.e., when private sector airlines like Buddha Air and Shree Airlines, along with Indian aircraft, are allowed to fly from cities like Delhi, the number of flights and seat capacity will increase significantly. With healthy competition in the market, airfares will naturally become cheaper.

Currently, due to limited flights, the Kathmandu-Delhi airfare is extremely expensive, which makes some tourists hesitate to come by air even if they want to. As soon as fares become cheaper and flights become easier, the arrival of Indian tourists to Nepal will increase unprecedentedly.

Similarly, after the opening of the Mahendranagar route, tourists from Europe and the Middle East will also be able to come directly to Pokhara and Bhairahawa (Lumbini) in a shorter time and at a lower cost. This will bring a significant positive ripple effect to Nepal's tourism business, hotel industry, travel agencies, and the local economy. Overall, the improvement in air routes and air connectivity has the potential to take Nepal's tourism and economy to new heights.

India's proposed Bagdogra route should be immediately subjected to a detailed technical study by the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and a team of aviation experts. If it does not have any significant impact on Nepal's air traffic and safety, then a concrete agreement should be reached to bring the Mahendranagar air entry point into immediate implementation, even if it requires showing flexibility.

What kind of strategy do you think the Government of Nepal should adopt to bring these issues to a conclusion in the Prime Minister's visit to India and upcoming diplomatic and technical negotiations?

The Government of Nepal should not limit these aviation sector issues to mere formal agendas but should pursue result-oriented diplomatic initiatives. Firstly, a detailed technical study of India's proposed Bagdogra route should be immediately conducted by the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and a team of aviation experts. If it does not have any significant impact on Nepal's air traffic and safety, then a concrete agreement should be reached to bring the Mahendranagar air entry point into immediate implementation, even if it requires showing flexibility. The commitment made 12 years ago must now be seen in practice, not just in documents and speeches.

Furthermore, to remove the inequality in air connectivity between Nepal and India, diplomatic pressure and dialogue should be intensified to immediately grant written flight permits to Nepali private airline companies like Buddha Air, Shree Airlines, etc., to fly to Delhi and other Indian cities. And along with external diplomatic efforts, internal plans for decentralization of necessary labor, immigration, and tourism-related services and effective marketing to operate the Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports at full capacity should also be implemented simultaneously.

India’s newly appointed Ambassador to Nepal, Sudhakar Dalela, today paid a courtesy call on Nepal’s Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, in Kathmandu.

During the meeting, the two sides discussed various aspects of India-Nepal cooperation in the energy and water resources sectors.

The discussions covered ongoing cooperation in hydropower projects, transmission infrastructure and cross-border electricity trade. Solar energy, water resources and water management were also among the issues discussed.

Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha welcomed Ambassador Dalela and conveyed his best wishes for a successful tenure.

The meeting reaffirmed the commitment of both countries to further strengthen bilateral cooperation and advance initiatives of mutual interest.

TROY - A Hudson Valley Community College student launched a fundraiser Tuesday to support her home country of Nepal, where communities continue to grapple with the effects of devastating floods that struck in August.

Kabita Karki, who is pursuing a degree in human services, told a room of attendees that she was grateful for the opportunity to "bring part of Nepal's story into this community."

As videos of the flooding played in the background, Karki cautioned against the world moving on from a disaster whose effects are still felt daily by those closest to her.

"We cannot ignore the bigger picture," Karki said. "Nepal is a country of incredible natural beauty, but many communities are vulnerable to floods, landslides and changing rainfall patterns. These challenges affect people's ability to earn a living, and when people lose their livelihoods, they may be forced to make difficult decisions about their future."

Nearly three months after floodwaters rushed through the Himalayan nation's villages along its border with China, thousands of Nepalese and Tibetan individuals have been reported dead or missing. Karki said those figures likely underestimate the human cost of the disaster.

Karki also highlighted how flooding has accelerated migration within Nepal, increasing pressure on rural residents to relocate to urban areas in search of greater opportunity and protection from disaster. That trend has intensified over the past decade, particularly following a 2015 earthquake that killed more than 8,000 people and injured more than 21,000. She added that the search for opportunity has prompted many to migrate beyond Nepal's borders as well.

The devastating effects of extreme weather continue to reverberate across Nepal, underscoring the vulnerability of communities facing increasingly severe climate-related disasters.

"This is why disaster recovery matters beyond the immediate emergency," Karki said. "Helping people rebuild their lives can also protect their future choices. We want people to have the opportunity to live with dignity, security and hope wherever they choose."

The Blue Butterfly Foundation, a Hudson Valley-based nonprofit that leads work in Nepal, is accepting funds for Nepalese flood victims. (Will Waldron/Times Union)

The local effort is unfolding against a broader international backdrop, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish city of Antalya this week to discuss climate change and the global response to its growing impact at the United Nations climate summit, known as COP31. The 12-day summit drew 197 nations; however, for the second consecutive year, the United States does not have an official government delegation in attendance.

At the summit, leaders from Nepal and other mountain nations have warned the world that there is no time to wait, sounding the alarm about future disasters from global temperature rise. So far, the United Nations has pledged $20 million in assistance.

For Karki and many of the roughly 20,000 Nepalese people living across New York, that figure represents the beginning of an investment in their home nation and the people they love who still live there.

Finding support

The week before her fall semester classes were set to begin, Karki saw news of the flooding in her home country. She remembers receiving a call from a friend in Nepal whose entire community had been affected.

Karki said she felt incredibly alone, watching a crisis unfold at home from the United States. As the full impact of the flooding has become clearer over the past three months, she said, it has reminded her of how vulnerable her home country is. She thinks about her mother, who recently underwent heart surgery, and the uncertainty facing other family members who still live there.

The crisis also reminded Karki of her own childhood experiences of trauma. Those experiences are what first connected her with the Blue Butterfly Foundation, a Hudson Valley-based nonprofit that leads work in Nepal. Now, Karki is leading a local fundraiser through that same organization to help protect and support those facing new or compounded vulnerabilities in the aftermath of the floods.

The fundraiser's $30,000 goal is divided among three areas of need: safe housing, mental health services and schools. Donations can be made online.

Hudson Valley Community College President Michael S. Brophy listens to Karki's talk. (Will Waldron/Times Union)

"I've always been passionate about helping people - it brings me peace," Karki said. "I especially want to help women, because being a woman and having been through a lot of trauma myself, I want to show them we are here for them."

That desire ultimately led Karki to pursue a degree in human services. In light of the recent floods, she is particularly concerned about the long-term mental health effects of the crisis, which she says will be felt across generations.

"We often talk about the physical destruction caused by disasters, but we don't talk enough about what happens inside a person," Karki said. "These people need trauma-informed care and professionals who can help them process what they have experienced."

That is especially important for young children in Nepal, Karki said, who may not fully understand what has happened. That concern informed her decision to contribute a portion of the funds raised to rebuilding schools.

It is not the first local fundraiser to benefit the Himalayan nation. In the immediate aftermath of the floods, the Albany New York Nepalese Society organized donations from the Capital Region's nearly 600-person community, partly in response to the Nepalese government's appeal to citizens living abroad to contribute to disaster relief.

But for Karki, the most poignant aspect of the disaster is the disruption of "home" for thousands of people in her native country. She explained that beyond a physical structure, home is a feeling of belonging, one that has been shaken for Nepalese people who live around the world.

As Karki put it, when people in Nepal are hurting, Nepalese communities everywhere feel pain.

title: Apple harvest reaches 5,500 tons in Nepal's Humla district - FreshPlaza
description: Apple harvest reaches 5,500 tons in Nepal's Humla district  FreshPlaza
publisher.title: FreshPlaza
full_article:
Apple growers in Nepal's Humla district harvested around 5,500 tons of apples this year, with 1,466 tons sold outside the district, according to the Agriculture Development Office.

The harvest came from 690 hectares of fruit-bearing orchards across seven rural municipalities. Recorded apple sales totaled Rs. 87.96 million (approximately US$585,307), based on an average farmgate price of Rs. 60 (US$0.40) per kilogram.

In July, district authorities introduced a requirement for growers to obtain recommendations from agricultural technicians before transporting apples outside Humla, aiming to prevent shipments of unripe fruit.

Reported shipments included 500 tons from Sarkegad, 400 tons from Simkot, 200 tons from Kharpunath, 140 tons from Chankheli, 50 tons from Namkha, 20 tons from Adanchuli, and 67.6 tons from Tajakot.

Actual sales may be higher because unregistered shipments, local transactions, and domestic consumption were excluded from the figures.

Last year, apple exports from the district were valued at around Rs. 40 million (approximately US$266,170) following the establishment of road connectivity.

District prices were set at Rs. 60 (US$0.40) per kilogram for Grade A apples, Rs. 50 (US$0.33) for Grade B, and Rs. 40 (US$0.27) for Grade C. Growers also sold eight tons of Fuji apples for the first time.

title: Nepal Proposes Separate Mountain Climate Program at COP-31 - Ratopati
description: Nepal Proposes Separate Mountain Climate Program at COP-31  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Antalya (Turkiye). Nepal is going to present a three-point proposal in the draft decision of COP-31 to operate a separate program on mountain regions and climate change from 2027 and to clarify its scope and implementation methods.

The draft decision, prepared in consultation with the presidency of COP-31, includes a proposal to establish a separate mountain climate program with the objective of addressing the risks faced by communities dependent on mountain regions and glaciers due to climate change.

While Nepal welcomed the proposal, it stated that important aspects of program implementation are not clear and further arrangements are needed. According to Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, Joint Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment and Chief of the Climate Change Management Division, Nepal will propose the timeline for the program to start from 2027, its scope and implementation methods, and specific indicators for mountain climate finance and adaptation.

The draft, prepared after consulting with the member states under the presidency of COP-31, includes a proposal in point 31 to establish a separate program on mountain regions and climate change. The program aims to enhance scientific understanding, adaptation actions, build resilience, and support communities dependent on mountains and glaciers.

The draft also proposes to include the issue of mountain regions and climate change in the permanent agenda of the Conference of the Parties (COP) and to organize a high-level dialogue at COP-32. Point 32 mentions organizing a dialogue on this issue in the 66th and 68th sessions of the subsidiary bodies and continuing it. Furthermore, it encourages regular high-level dialogues to include the priorities of mountain countries, indigenous, and local communities in climate action.

These proposals included in the draft are seen as progress in Nepal's efforts to institutionalize mountain issues in the United Nations climate negotiations. However, the issues jointly put forward by Nepal and Bhutan on October 29 have not been fully included in the draft.

Abhishek Shrestha, advisor to the Minister of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, Geeta Chaudhary, welcomed the draft and said that further efforts will continue to include all the issues proposed by Nepal. He informed that negotiations are ongoing with the concerned countries and groups and expressed the expectation that the proposed issues will be included.

Nepal and Bhutan had jointly put forward a proposal on October 29 to include the issue of keeping the temperature rise in the Himalayan region within the limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius in the separate agenda of COP-31. Both countries made the proposal to make the risks arising from climate change in the Himalayan region a major topic of international climate negotiations. Minister Chaudhary had presented the proposal on behalf of Nepal and Bhutan under rule 12 of the draft working procedures of the conference.

title: Agroecological Farming Matches Or Exceeds Conventional Vegetable Yields In Nepal Study - Bioengineer.org
description: Agroecological Farming Matches Or Exceeds Conventional Vegetable Yields In Nepal Study  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
In an extensive matched observational study across smallholder vegetable systems in Nepal, a locally adapted agroecological management package demonstrated productivity and gross revenues that matched or exceeded conventional farming during early transition. Published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems by researchers from Nepal and the Republic of Korea, the investigation evaluated paired farm plots managed by smallholders in three contrasting environments: Lalitpur, Humla, and Doti. Analyzing 242 complete within-farmer pairs representing 484 plot observations across seven crop-site combinations between May 2023 and January 2024, the study found that farmers adopting the package achieved positive yield differences across all evaluated crops. Statistically significant productivity gains occurred in five combinations, and no crop exhibited a measurable yield penalty. Furthermore, gross revenues were significantly higher on agroecological plots in six of the seven combinations, challenging assumptions that smallholders inevitably face immediate economic penalties during early transition.

The research addressed widespread biophysical and socioeconomic vulnerabilities confronting smallholder agriculture across Nepal. Agrarian systems throughout the country face persistent challenges stemming from soil degradation, steep terrain erosion, climate variability, and heavy dependence on external inputs. Across South Asia, mineral fertilizer applications have escalated in recent decades, establishing synthetic nitrogen and phosphorus as dominant regional nutrient sources, while smaller nations like Nepal retained greater reliance on livestock manure. Because Nepal possesses no domestic fertilizer manufacturing facilities, national supplies regularly fail to satisfy demand, with official data indicating that chemical supplies in 2018/2019 covered only about sixty percent of effective national requirements. In hill and mountain farming systems, transport bottlenecks, fluctuating input prices, and soil erosion severely threaten rural livelihoods and food security, prompting researchers to examine whether regenerative, low-external-input systems can provide stable agronomic returns across diverse topographies.

To address these constraints, the evaluated program introduced a locally adapted system known as natural farming, designed to replace commercial synthetic products with biological management and on-farm resource recycling. The agroecological package integrated four core components: reduced or zero tillage to safeguard soil structure, organic mulching using crop residues to conserve moisture and suppress weeds, aerobic livestock compost as a primary basal soil amendment, and farmer-prepared biological inputs. These specialized liquid formulations included Indigenous Microorganisms cultured from forest soils, Fermented Plant Juice, Fermented Fruit Juice, Oriental Herbal Nutrient extracts containing ginger and garlic, Fish Amino Acids, eggshell calcium solutions, bone phosphorus solutions, diluted cow urine, and rice-washing water. Because published scientific literature on individual farm-made formulations remains limited, the study evaluated the package strictly as an integrated agroecological system rather than attributing outcomes to isolated preparations.

A vital element of the study was its documentation of baseline conventional practices across the three project districts. In Lalitpur and Doti, conventional farming reflected typical semi-commercial production, incorporating tillage, residue removal without mulching, and routine applications of synthetic fertilizers like urea, diammonium phosphate, and potash, alongside chemical pesticides including cypermethrin, dichlorvos, and mancozeb. In contrast, conventional farming in the remote high-Himalayan district of Humla represented an established low-input system relying exclusively on manual hoeing and livestock manure, with zero recorded synthetic fertilizer or pesticide use. Consequently, comparisons in Lalitpur and Doti evaluated the direct substitution of synthetic chemicals by agroecological methods, whereas the comparison in Humla tested whether structured zero-tillage, surface mulching, and fermented botanical inputs offered performance advantages over traditional low-input organic management rather than chemical agriculture.

The quantitative sampling framework originated from a baseline survey of 1,659 smallholder farmers across twelve districts conducted between December 2022 and April 2023. From 2,058 smallholders who completed training delivered by Good Neighbors International Nepal, researchers selected 314 farmers across nineteen cooperatives for productivity and revenue monitoring. The final statistical sample was restricted to 242 complete within-farmer pairs across Lalitpur, Humla, and Doti after screening out four incomplete records. Under this paired design, each participating farmer simultaneously managed an agroecological plot and a conventional plot of the same crop during the same production period. Plots were situated on the same holding or generally within one hundred meters to minimize spatial and microclimatic heterogeneity. Because plot areas, recorded in local ropani units, were not completely balanced between systems, all harvest and sales data were standardized to per-hectare values.

To analyze plot records without assuming experimental randomization, the authors utilized Gaussian linear mixed-effects models fitted via restricted maximum likelihood. The analytical framework specified the farming system as a fixed effect and the matched farmer pair as a random intercept, rendering the estimated treatment coefficient algebraically equivalent to the mean paired difference. Hypothesis testing and ninety-five percent confidence intervals relied on Student’s t-distribution with finite-sample degrees of freedom. Standardized effect sizes were calculated using Cohen’s dz, while variance partitioning was examined using marginal and conditional R-squared values. In addition, the researchers conducted sensitivity analyses using modified z-scores to screen for influential outliers, confirming that primary findings remained stable when extreme observations were excluded. The authors emphasized that because plot allocation was observational, all statistical estimates represent within-pair associations rather than causal treatment effects.

Across the seven crop-site combinations, empirical productivity results showed that the agroecological package delivered competitive yields, recording positive point estimates in every setting. Statistically significant productivity advantages emerged in five combinations: Lalitpur cauliflower produced an additional 3.92 metric tons per hectare under agroecological management, Humla cauliflower yielded 3.86 metric tons per hectare more, Humla tomato gained 3.77 metric tons per hectare, Humla potato increased by 1.95 metric tons per hectare, and Doti cucurbits gained 0.57 metric tons per hectare over conventional plots. In the remaining two strata, Lalitpur broadleaf mustard and Lalitpur tomato showed positive mean differences of 0.96 and 0.97 metric tons per hectare, respectively, but these did not reach statistical significance. Crucially, across all monitored environments, no crop exhibited a statistically significant productivity disadvantage under the agroecological regime during the monitored season.

Financial analyses of gross revenue revealed substantial advantages for the agroecological package, with significantly higher revenues recorded in six of the seven crop-site combinations. In Lalitpur, agroecological cauliflower generated an average revenue gain of 133.7 thousand Nepalese rupees per hectare, broadleaf mustard generated an additional 134.8 thousand rupees per hectare, and tomato achieved a premium of 2,196.9 thousand rupees per hectare. In Humla, gross revenues were significantly higher on agroecological plots for cauliflower by 171.3 thousand rupees per hectare and for potato by 92.0 thousand rupees per hectare, while Doti cucurbits achieved an increase of 38.8 thousand rupees per hectare. Humla tomato was the sole exception, where a revenue gain of 39.4 thousand rupees per hectare was not statistically significant despite large yield increases. The authors noted that gross revenue measures crop sales before deducting operational expenses, meaning financial differentials cannot be interpreted as net farm profits.

The investigation also identified notable localized variation within smaller administrative units, particularly between two agricultural cooperatives in Lalitpur cultivating broadleaf mustard. When data were examined separately for each cooperative, representing twenty-five matched pairs each, contrasting patterns appeared. Farmers belonging to the Saraswoti Kunda Agriculture Cooperative achieved a statistically significant productivity gain of 2.49 metric tons per hectare and a gross revenue increase of 249.3 thousand rupees per hectare under the agroecological package. Conversely, members of the Sarangeedada Women Agriculture Cooperative experienced no significant differences in either outcome, recording a slight yield difference of minus 0.58 metric tons per hectare and a revenue difference of 20.4 thousand rupees per hectare. Because organizational capacity, market access, and extension support were not measured as explanatory variables, the authors cautioned that these cooperative differences demonstrate contextual heterogeneity rather than established organizational causes.

Complementary economic and qualitative findings emerged from baseline household financial data and twenty-seven key informant interviews. Among 513 baseline households reporting chemical input use outside Humla, annual input expenditures averaged 15,463 rupees per household, including 4,002 rupees for chemical fertilizers, 1,501 rupees for pesticides, 722 rupees for micronutrients, and 429 rupees for irrigation, alongside 4,696 rupees for hired labor. Among twenty-two interviewed farmers in chemical-using districts, respondents reported median savings of 4,000 rupees per ropani under the agroecological package, primarily attributed to reduced labor for tillage and weeding, as well as lower irrigation needs. Thematic analysis showed that all twenty-seven key informants reported lower purchased-input costs and reduced irrigation needs, while twenty-six noted reduced labor demands and twenty-two reported improved soil condition. However, perceptions of productivity and market demand varied significantly by location, with several farmers reporting no price premiums for agroecological produce.

In assessing broader implications, the authors highlighted critical limitations that constrain causal interpretation. Because plots were not randomly assigned, residual confounding from baseline soil fertility, historical land management, and microclimatic factors cannot be ruled out despite within-farmer pairing. Furthermore, monitoring was restricted to a single production season, preventing conclusions regarding long-term soil health, multi-year yield stability, or resilience under extreme weather events. The lack of standardized price data, crop grade records, and comprehensive accounting of family labor spent preparing biological mixtures also precludes conclusions regarding net profitability or household disposable income. While maintaining productivity and reducing chemical reliance offer promising conceptual links to food security and sovereignty, the researchers concluded that multi-season longitudinal studies with direct soil measurements and complete cost accounting are essential to verify whether agroecological transitions remain sustainable across smallholder farming systems in the Himalayan region.

title: Enhance economic integration between Nepal, India: Experts - The Rising Nepal
description: Enhance economic integration between Nepal, India: Experts  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter

Kathmandu, Nov. 18: Experts suggested that Nepal and India should enhance bilateral cooperation in energy and infrastructure connectivity, and strengthen economic integration.

Speaking at a discussion on 'Contemporary Nepal-India Relations' organised -- on the eve of Prime Minister Balendra Shah's anticipated visit to India -- by the Centre for Social Innovation and Foreign Policy (CESIF) in Kathmandu on Tuesday, they also emphasised on exploring new and emerging areas of cooperation and strengthening institutional mechanisms and implementation.

The speakers underlined the need to move beyond historical political sensitivities, mistrust and dependency narratives towards a relationship based on mutual respect, equality and shared interests.

Former Ambassador of India to Nepal Ranjit Rae highlighted the importance of the Prime Minister’s upcoming visit to India in building mutual trust through direct engagement and face-to-face interactions. He also called for expanding bilateral cooperation into new areas, particularly climate change and its growing impacts, recalling India’s humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR) support to Nepal following the earthquake and the Bhotekoshi disaster.

Stating that the multilateral system is under strain, with ongoing conflicts and global developments increasingly affecting the interests of both countries, Ambassador Rae called for Nepal and India to work together to address these shared challenges.

He described the emergence of a new generation of dynamic leaders, focused on the country’s economic development and unburdened by the political baggage of the past, as a moment of hope for Nepal and an opportunity to advance bilateral relations.

Likewise, Former Vice Chairperson of the National Planning Commission, Dr. Govind Pokharel, said that it is important to alignin Nepal’s development priorities with India’s economic growth and infrastructure development. According to him, there are further opportunities to expand cooperation in energy, trade, agriculture, and connectivity.

"There is a need to facilitate private sector participation in cross-border electricity trade, attract greater Indian investment in hydropower, and move forward with long-pending projects by resolving outstanding issues related to water sharing and the distribution of costs and benefits," said Dr. Pokharel. He also called for improved air connectivity, mutually recognised quality-testing laboratories to facilitate agricultural trade, and better arrangements for cross-border migrant workers.

Speaking on the occasion, General Anil Chauhan, former Chief of Defence Staff and Director of the Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF), India, said that bilateral relations are increasingly shaped by evolving regional security dynamics, shifting national interests, technological advances, and the changing relationship between major powers.

Stressing to broaden bilateral engagement beyond government-to-government interactions, he called for stronger collaboration among think tanks, academia, and civil society.

He noted that the bilateral relationship must remain grounded in equality, mutual respect, and sensitivity towards Nepal’s independent identity and sovereignty.

Former Chief Advisor to the Prime Minister and Research Director at CESIF, Ajaya Bhadra Khanal, said that while anti-Indian nationalism has periodically shaped Nepal’s domestic politics, particularly since the 2015 Constitution, the country remains dependent on cooperation with India to advance economic development.

"Despite these political differences, the past decade has seen considerable progress in physical connectivity, infrastructure and bilateral agreements, creating an opportunity to move Nepal-India relations into a new phase," he said.

However, he said that greater connectivity and duty-free access have not necessarily translated into improved market access for Nepali goods, contributing to the growing trade deficit and economic dependency.

Khanal pointed out the necessity to shift the focus from competing with India to integrating into its value chains, particularly in neighbouring states such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Uttarakhand. This would require harmonising standards, addressing non-tariff barriers, attracting Indian investment, promoting joint ventures and strengthening cooperation in hydropower, digital services and tourism.

Similarly, Arpita Nepal, Co-founder of Samriddhi Foundation, questioned viewing foreign capital through a dependency lens.

She urged policymakers to harmonize tariffs, enforce intellectual property rights, and review Nepal's rigid labour laws alongside cross-border labour discrepancies. She also proposed evaluating energy investments through climate adaptation and a broader coalition across the Himalayan range, enacting data-sovereignty and privacy laws aligned with India.

"Complex tariffs and protectionist rules breed rent-seeking ties between political elites and favoured firms, while simple, cross-border-aligned rules attract productive capital without costly oversight," said Nepal.

Former commerce secretary Purushottam Ojha said that while tariffs have largely receded under duty-free provisions, mutual irritants still hold back trade. "Nepali exporters face non-tariff hurdles on tea, quota-restricted items, and jute products hit by both anti-dumping duties and labelling rules," he said adding that Indian officials raise concerns over Nepal's agricultural reform fee, erosion of tariff preferences, trademark and intellectual property violations, and informal border trade.

According to Ojha, focus should be on export growth, tourism services, electricity, digital trade, and specialty farm goods rather than bulk crops. He recommended revising the current Treaty of Trade into a broader agreement covering investment, trade facilitation, production sharing, customs cooperation, SMEs, and binding dispute resolution.

Maj. Gen. Binoj Basnyat (Rtd.) said that the two countries do not need more bilateral bodies beyond the 40-plus mechanisms, and should instead consolidate overlapping groups, set measurable priorities, and escalate technical deadlocks to political leaders.

He proposed institutionalising an annual Prime Ministers' summit rotating across cities in Nepal and India atop a four-tier execution structure with a joint implementation review mechanism.

Anurag Acharya, a researcher, suggested turning existing agreements on Integrated Check Posts (ICPs), pipelines, railways, energy, air connectivity, and cross-border entry points into timely, visible outcomes with clear schedules.

He also urged expanding economic ties beyond hydropower into niche investments, including food processing, agro-based goods, Himalayan herbs, timber industries in Nepal's mid-hills, and cricket infrastructure to spur tourism.
